# Cardiac Amyloidosis: A Narrative Review

## Introduction and Epidemiology

Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy resulting from the extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils within the myocardium. Cardiac amyloidosis is caused by deposition of amyloid fibrils in the myocardium and has two main subtypes, transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis (ATTR) and immunoglobulin light chain cardiac amyloidosis (AL). [1] ATTR is further subclassified: ATTR is further differentiated into wild-type (wtATTR) and hereditary (hATTR), depending on the absence or presence of mutation in the transthyretin gene. [1] Once considered rare and untreatable, the disease has been transformed by improved recognition and effective therapy. The increased recognition of disease with the improvement in diagnostic armamentarium and serendipitous advancements in the therapeutic landscape have changed the status of CA from being a rare and untreatable disease to being a not-so-rare and treatable disease. [1]

The condition is substantially underdiagnosed, particularly in older adults with heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). In a prospective screening study, the study included 120 HFpEF patients, and a total of 16 patients (13.3%) showed a moderate-to-severe uptake on the 99mTc-DPD scintigraphy, identifying wild-type ATTR as an important contributor to HFpEF [2]. Autopsy data reinforce this, with one series finding cardiac amyloidosis in 104 of 1972 autopsies (5%) with 91% neither diagnosed nor suspected ante mortem [3]. Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) is an under-recognized cause of heart failure (HF) in older adults, resulting from myocardial deposition of misfolded transthyretin (TTR) or pre-albumin. [4]

## Clinical Presentation and Pathophysiology

Amyloid infiltration produces a restrictive cardiomyopathy with progressive diastolic and later systolic dysfunction. ATTR-cardiomyopathy can occur in the context of genetically normal protein (wild type or ATTRwt-CM) or due to genetic mutations (most commonly isoleucine substitution for valine at position 122), rendering the protein abnormal (ATTRv-CM). [5] Because amyloid is a multisystem disorder, since amyloid fibrils can deposit in multiple organs, multidisciplinary care is a requisite. [5] Clinical clues include increased left ventricular hypertrophy in the absence of hypertension or valvular heart disease, heart failure symptoms, diastolic dysfunction, atrial fibrillation, and conduction system disease [5]. Untreated, the disease carries a grim prognosis, being fatal within a median of 2–6 years if untreated [6].

## Diagnosis

A defining advance has been the validation of non-invasive diagnosis. In a landmark multicenter study, technetium-labeled bone scintigraphy was shown to localize to myocardial ATTR deposits, demonstrating that the bone-seeking radionuclide tracers 99mTc-DPD, 99mTc-HMDP, and 99mTc-pyrophosphate have high sensitivity for cardiac transthyretin deposits and can differentiate from immunoglobulin light chain amyloidosis [7]. This approach addressed a longstanding problem, since the diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed because of the limited specificity of echocardiography and the traditional requirement for histological confirmation [7]. Crucially, ATTR can now be diagnosed without biopsy when grade 2–3 cardiac uptake is present alongside the exclusion of a monoclonal protein.

Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) provides complementary tissue characterization. Cardiac transthyretin amyloidosis is an increasingly recognized cause of heart failure, and CMR with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and T1 mapping is emerging as a reference standard for diagnosis and characterization, with extracellular volume fraction (ECV) used to characterize cardiac involvement in relation to outcome [8]. Native T1 mapping and ECV reflect distinct biology between subtypes; ECV detects cardiac ATTR amyloid with similar diagnostic performance to T1, the ECV is higher in TTR (proportionately more amyloid than in AL hearts), yet the native T1 is lower [9]. Comprehensive multidisciplinary frameworks for diagnosis and staging have been codified in consensus documents [10,11].

## Disease-Modifying Therapy

### Transthyretin stabilizers

The therapeutic era began with tafamidis. Transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy is caused by the deposition of transthyretin amyloid fibrils in the myocardium; the deposition occurs when wild-type or variant transthyretin becomes unstable and misfolds, and tafamidis binds to transthyretin, preventing tetramer dissociation and amyloidogenesis. [12] In the pivotal ATTR-ACT trial, the protein stabilizer tafamidis resulted in a 13.4% absolute reduction in overall mortality and a 22% absolute reduction in yearly cardiovascular hospitalization at 30 months compared to placebo [12]. A subsequent oral stabilizer, acoramidis, extended this class. In clinical trials, acoramidis demonstrated statistically significant reductions in the composite of all-cause mortality or first cardiovascular-related hospitalization evident within 3 months and sustained through 30 months [13].

### TTR gene silencers

RNA-targeting therapeutics reduce hepatic TTR production. In the APOLLO-B trial, an international, phase 3, multicenter, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trial of patisiran in patients with variant or wild-type ATTR cardiac amyloidosis, patisiran, an RNAi therapeutic targeting transthyretin, preserved functional capacity and health status and quality of life compared with placebo at 12 months [14]. The subcutaneous agent vutrisiran built on this; the HELIOS-B trial showed that vutrisiran was effective at preventing deaths and adverse events among patients with ATTR-CM [15], in a population in which patients were randomized to vutrisiran 25 mg vs. placebo every 12 weeks, and could remain on tafamidis if already on this medication at enrollment [15].

### AL amyloidosis

For light-chain disease, treatment targets the clonal plasma cells. In the ANDROMEDA trial, in patients with newly diagnosed AL amyloidosis, the addition of subcutaneous daratumumab to bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone resulted in significantly better outcomes [16], with hematologic complete response achieved in 53.3% of the daratumumab arm vs 18.1% of the control arm [17]. Cardiac stage strongly influences AL prognosis [18], and earlier RNAi work in hereditary ATTR with polyneuropathy established proof of concept for TTR knockdown [19].

## Conclusions

CA has been redefined from an orphan disease into a treatable cause of heart failure, owing to non-invasive imaging diagnosis [7,20], refined risk staging [21], and multiple effective disease-modifying therapies. Early recognition remains paramount, as emerging therapies that stabilize TTR have been shown to improve outcomes, and early diagnosis will be critical to afford the best efficacy of therapies [4]. Heightened clinical suspicion in elderly HFpEF patients, aortic stenosis, and unexplained left ventricular hypertrophy should prompt timely evaluation [22–30].
